warmup.q: The new store files payments under a two-part address: first the account, then the time. It can jump straight to one account, and inside it, read payments in time order. You ask for shop M-0042's payments from today, and the address says nothing about shops. What can the store do?
options: Use the index it builds by itself on every field
Read every payment on every machine and keep M-0042's, unless you add a second copy of the data filed by shop
Turn M-0042 into a machine number, the way it does with any key
Read only today's payments, because the time is part of the address
warmup.why: Only a value for the first part of the address tells the store which machine to go to. A shop's id says nothing about where accounts live, so turning it into a machine number finds the wrong place. Stores like this build no indexes unless you ask, and the time only orders payments inside one account. So the choice is a read of everything, called a scan, or a second copy of the data filed by shop. This lesson is about making that choice before the first payment arrives.

sections.h: A store spread over many machines finds data only by its key
sections.html:
Let's start with what PostgreSQL does. You can filter on any column: WHERE merchant_id = 4 runs even without an index. The database reads the whole table from its own disk, and if that's too slow, you add an index and the database starts using it. One machine holds everything, so there's always a way.

Now spread 50 million payments over 40 partitions on 40 machines. A partition, as in Why other data models exist, is one slice of the data, held by one machine or a small group of machines. A query that doesn't say which partition holds its answer has to ask all 40, and each one reads everything it holds.

DynamoDB and Cassandra refuse to work that way unless you insist. DynamoDB is a database that Amazon's cloud business, AWS, runs for its customers. Cassandra is a free database, first built at Facebook, that companies run on their own machines. Both find data by key, and only by key, so you design the key around the questions.

A supermarket has the same problem. Its shelves are arranged by kind, so all the pasta is in one aisle. "Everything on special offer today" means walking every aisle, because the shelves aren't arranged by offer.

Let's build a key for one question: "account A-1001's 20 newest payments".

Version 1 keys each payment by its payment id. The store hashes the id, turning it into a number that picks the partition, the way Dynamo did in the last lesson. Fetching one payment by id touches one partition and one item, the store's name for one record. But A-1001's payments are scattered over all 40 partitions, so the question has to visit all 40.

Version 2 keys each payment by its account id. All of A-1001's payments now share a key, so they land in the same partition. This part of the key is the partition key. The store hashes it, so it can only answer "equals this value", and only when you give all of it. A busy account has 30,000 payments, though, and inside the partition nothing says which are the newest. The store would read all 30,000 and sort them to return 20.

Version 3 adds a second part to the key, the sort key, here the time the payment was created. Inside a partition, the store keeps items sorted by it, as Bigtable keeps rows sorted. "The 20 newest" becomes: go to A-1001's partition, start at the end, step back 20 items. Every item now has an address in two parts: the partition key says which partition, the sort key says where inside it. That's the picture for this lesson. Every design below is a choice of address.

The address gives every query one of three outcomes:

  • A key lookup gives the whole address with =. On the table, that's one item.
  • A range read gives the partition key with = and a range or an order on the sort key. It reads one run of neighbouring items, and its cost grows with what it returns.
  • A scan is everything else. The store reads items and throws some away: at best one whole partition, at worst the whole table.

The demo below puts 200,000 payments in one sorted map and counts what each kind of question touches. Then we'll make every question the app needs a lookup or a range read.

try.title: Count what each question touches
steps: Read AccessPathDemo.kt. It loads 200,000 made-up payments into one TreeMap, a map that keeps its keys sorted, keyed accountId#createdAt#paymentId. That's how a store keeps items sorted inside its partitions. The shop is only in the value, not in the key.
Predict how many entries each question touches: one payment by its full key, account A-00042's newest 20, and all of shop M-0042's payments.

code.title: AccessPathDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l02.demo import java.util.TreeMap /** The key of payment number i: accountId # createdAt # paymentId. */ private fun keyOf(i: Int): String { val account = "A-%05d".format(i % 10_000) val createdAt = "2026-11-%02dT%02d:%02d".format(1 + i % 7, (i / 7) % 24, (i / 168) % 60) return "$account#$createdAt#pay-$i" } /** 200,000 payments in one sorted map, keyed account#time#payment. Three questions, three costs. */ fun main() { // the value is the merchant, which is NOT part of the key val payments = TreeMap<String, String>() for (i in 0 until 200_000) payments[keyOf(i)] = "M-%04d".format(i % 997) fun timed(label: String, block: () -> Pair<Int, Int>) { var result = 0 to 0 val nanos = (1..21).map { // run it 21 times, report the median val t0 = System.nanoTime() result = block() System.nanoTime() - t0 }.sorted()[10] println("%-34s found %4d, touched %,7d entries, about %,9d ns".format(label, result.first, result.second, nanos)) } // 1. the full key: one lookup val oneKey = keyOf(160_042) timed("key lookup (full key)") { (if (payments[oneKey] != null) 1 else 0) to 1 } // 2. the account is the key's prefix: one contiguous slice, read from the end for newest first timed("A-00042's newest 20 (range read)") { val slice = payments.subMap("A-00042#", true, "A-00042$", false).descendingMap() // '$' comes right after '#' val newest = slice.entries.take(20) newest.size to newest.size } // 3. the merchant is not in the key: nothing to jump to, so look at everything timed("merchant M-0042's payments (scan)") { var touched = 0 var found = 0 for ((_, merchant) in payments) { touched++ if (merchant == "M-0042") found++ } found to touched } }

try.expect:
key lookup (full key)              found    1, touched       1 entries, about       625 ns
A-00042's newest 20 (range read)   found   20, touched      20 entries, about    14,208 ns
merchant M-0042's payments (scan)  found  201, touched 200,000 entries, about 3,683,584 ns

The entry counts are exact. The times are from one run on a laptop with an Apple M-series chip. They move with your computer, and with how far the JVM (the program that runs Kotlin) has warmed up, since it speeds code up as it runs it. The shop question has only 201 answers, but the map touches all 200,000 entries to find them, a few hundred times slower than the range read. Load a million payments, and the range read still touches 20; the scan touches a million.

aside.title: Couldn't all 40 machines search their part at the same time?
aside.html: They could, and some stores do. It's still slow, for three reasons. Every machine reads everything it holds, so the total work grows with the table, not with the answer. The question is only as fast as the slowest of the 40, the tail from Latency, percentiles and the tail, so one busy machine makes every such question late. And each question keeps all 40 machines busy, so 200 questions a second become 8,000 partition reads a second.

sections.h: Write the questions down before you choose the keys
sections.html:
The key from the last section answers one question well. The payments app asks several, and one key can't answer them all. So the first thing to design is a list of the questions, each written as the query the code will send. Cassandra's documentation says it plainly: data modeling is query-driven. Each question on the list is called an access pattern. Here's the list every lab in this track uses:

# Access pattern As a query How often
AP1 An account's payments, newest first account = ?, order by time very often
AP2 A payment by its id payment id = ? very often
AP3 A shop's payments with one status in a time window shop = ?, status = ?, time between ? and ? often
AP4 Has this idempotency key been used? idempotency key = ? every new payment
AP5 A transfer between two accounts, with its lines in the account book two accounts, all or nothing often
AP6 The refunds of a payment payment id = ? rarely

An idempotency key is a code the card reader sends with each payment request, so the same request sent twice can be spotted. Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics, the next lesson, builds the check. Write each pattern with = for the values the code knows exactly, and a range or an order for the rest. Put a rate next to each. It tells you where a scan is fine, such as a nightly export, and where it isn't, such as the moment a card is tapped, thousands of times a second.

Then hold every pattern to one rule: it must be a key lookup or a range read. Check the first three against the address from the last section, partition key accountId and sort key createdAt. AP1 is a range read. AP2 gives a payment id, which isn't part of the address, so it's a scan. So is AP3.

When the address can't answer a pattern, you add a second copy of the data under a different address. DynamoDB calls that copy a global secondary index, and keeps it up to date for you. In Cassandra, it's another table that your code writes. In MongoDB, a document store, it's another index. In the supermarket, it's the special-offers stand by the door: the same products, arranged a second way, and every delivery now stocks two places. (The picture breaks there: a tin can only sit in one place, while data can be copied as often as you like.) Every copy costs one more write for every new payment. The stepper walks AP1 to AP3 through this design, one copy at a time.

Two rules decide whether a copy's sort key can serve a pattern, and both follow from the sorted run.

No gaps: the sort key is used from left to right. With the sort key (status, createdAt), items are sorted by status first, then by time. "FAILED since 09:00" is one run. "Any status since 09:00" is scattered across every status's run, so it isn't one read.

Filters cost what they read: a condition on a field outside the address, such as DynamoDB's FilterExpression, runs after the read. You pay for every item read, not every item returned.

This rigidity has a price. A new question next quarter can mean a new index, or rewriting old items to fill in a new key. Alex DeBrie, who wrote a well-known book on DynamoDB, lists that inflexibility among the costs of designing around keys. You pay it in exchange for reads that stay fast at any size. Next, we'll see a store that turns the no-gaps rule into an error message.

stepper.title: Three access patterns against one key design
stepper.intro: A payments table keyed by account and time. Watch which questions it answers, and what the fixes cost.

try.title: Predict the verdicts before the lab does
steps: Take the final design from the stepper: the table (accountId; createdAt), an index (merchantId; status, createdAt) and an index (paymentId). Before the semicolon is the partition key; after it, the sort key.

For each query, write down key lookup, range read or scan, and which table or index serves it: (a) accountId = A-1001 AND createdAt BETWEEN 08:00 AND 12:00; (b) merchantId = M-0042 AND createdAt > 09:00; (c) merchantId = M-0042 AND status = FAILED, newest first; (d) accountId = A-1001 AND currency = EUR; (e) paymentId = pay-81741; (f) status = FAILED.
try.expect: (a) Range read on the table. (b) Scan: it skips status, so it reads all of M-0042's partition and filters by time. (c) Range read on the shop index, read backward. (d) Scan: currency is outside every key, so it reads all of A-1001's items and filters. (e) Key lookup on the paymentId index. (f) Scan of everything, because status is never a partition key. Notice that (b) and (d) read one partition, not the whole table. That's cheaper than (f), but the cost still grows with the partition instead of with the answer, which is why the lab's checker calls it a scan too.

sections.h: Cassandra: one table for each question
sections.html:
Cassandra uses the same two-part address, and goes one step further: its query language refuses a query that doesn't follow it. The language is CQL (Cassandra Query Language). It looks like SQL, but a table's primary key is the address, written in two parts:

CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id   text,
    created_at   timestamp,
    payment_id   text,
    merchant_id  text,
    status       text,
    amount_minor bigint,
    currency     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC);

The inner parentheses hold the partition key, account_id. Cassandra hashes it onto its ring of machines, the way Dynamo did. The columns after it are clustering columns, Cassandra's name for the parts of the sort key. Here they're created_at, stored newest first, then payment_id, so two payments in the same millisecond don't overwrite each other. AP1 is now one partition read, already in the order the screen wants.

AP3 gets its own table, with an address built for the shop:

PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, day), status, created_at, payment_id)

The partition key has two parts this time. Without day, a busy shop taking 40,000 payments a day would grow one partition without end, and the Cassandra documentation advises keeping a partition under 100,000 values and 100 MB. Splitting by day has its own price: a week of history is seven partition reads.

The program writes every payment to both tables. That's normal here. Cassandra's modeling guide says it copies data on purpose, and leans on cheap writes to make reads fast. A Cassandra write is cheap because it's the LSM design from the last lesson: an append to a log, plus an insert into a sorted table in memory. Wide-column stores with Cassandra, lesson 5 of this track, watches it happen and sizes the day split properly.

Ask a table a question its address can't answer, and CQL stops you with an error that names the way out, ALLOW FILTERING. Add those words, and the query runs by reading partitions and filtering them, with performance the documentation calls unpredictable. Treat that error as a design review: a table is missing.

That's the café owner's error from the opening. Next, we'll meet a store that lets you index any field, and hands you a different question instead.

try.title: Make CQL refuse a query
steps: From the labs folder, start Cassandra 5.0: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait. Docker is a program that runs small separate machines, called containers, on your computer, and this command starts one with Cassandra inside. It takes about a minute to report healthy.

Load the two tables and six payments: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-02-payments.cql. cqlsh is Cassandra's command-line window, like psql. No output means it worked.
Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -k payments. Run the four queries below one at a time, and predict before each one whether it runs.
Stop Cassandra when you're done: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml down -v.

code.html: -- 1. AP1: one partition, already stored newest first SELECT created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_account WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' LIMIT 3; -- 2. the merchant is not in this table's key SELECT payment_id FROM payments_by_account WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042'; -- 3. AP3, on the table built for it SELECT status, created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND status = 'FAILED' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000'; -- 4. the same, but skip the status clustering column SELECT payment_id FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000';

Queries 1 and 3 run; 2 and 4 are refused (output trimmed):

---------------------------------+------------+--------------

sections.h: MongoDB: decide what goes inside one document
sections.html:
MongoDB lets you index any field, so you never have to squeeze every question into one address. The question it hands you instead is about shape: what goes inside one document, and what stands on its own.

MongoDB is a popular document store. A document is a record of named fields, written like JSON, whose fields can hold other objects and lists. MongoDB stores it in a binary form called BSON, and a group of documents is a collection, much like a table. Here's the choice for payments, as two collections:

// accounts: what the account screen shows, in one read
{ _id: "A-1001", customerId: "C-77", currency: "EUR",
  recentPayments: [ { id: "pay-81730", amountMinor: 4250 } /* the last 3 only */ ] }

// payments: one document each, pointing at its account
{ _id: "pay-81730", accountId: "A-1001", merchantId: "M-0043", status: "SETTLED",
  amountMinor: 4250, createdAt: ISODate("2026-11-07T10:30:12Z") }

Putting the recent payments inside the account is called embedding. Storing payments as their own documents, each holding its account's id, is called referencing. MongoDB's own guidance gives the rule. Embed what is read together, changed together, or belongs to its parent the way a line belongs to a receipt. Then one read returns it all, and a change to one document is atomic, all or nothing. Reference what has many entries, grows without end, is written at different times from the parent, or makes sense on its own.

Payments grow without end: an account keeps receiving them for years. Embed them all, and the account document grows toward MongoDB's 16 MB limit for one document, and every read of the account drags the whole history along. A short, capped summary gives the screen what it needs in one read. $push with $slice adds to the list and trims it to a fixed length in one update.

The two-part address comes back in the indexes. A compound index is a sorted list made from several fields, each entry pointing at its document, so it behaves like a sort key. MongoDB's ESR guideline orders its fields the same way as the no-gaps rule: fields you compare with = first (equality), then the field you sort by, then fields with a range. For AP3, { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 } (1 for ascending, -1 for descending) lets one walk of the index return a shop's FAILED payments, newest first. Leave status out of the query, and MongoDB can still use the index to find the shop, but it has to sort the results in memory. It's the same rule as in Cassandra, enforced by cost instead of by an error.

That's the limit of every design in this lesson, too. Each one answers the questions on the list, and a question nobody wrote down costs a scan or a new copy of the data.

try.title: Watch an index follow the access pattern
steps: From the labs folder, start MongoDB 9.0 in Docker: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml up -d --wait (a few seconds).

Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz (mongosh is MongoDB's command-line window), then load the data: load("/sfz/nosql-02-payments.js"). It writes 1,000 payments for 50 accounts and defines cost(), which asks MongoDB to explain how it ran a query and keeps four numbers from the answer.
Run the blocks below in order. Before each cost(...), predict how many documents MongoDB examines to return 5.
Stop MongoDB when you're done: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml down -v.

code.title: in mongosh
code.html: // embed a bounded summary: the account keeps only its last 3 payments for (const p of db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).sort({ createdAt: 1 }).limit(5)) { db.accounts.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001" }, { $push: { recentPayments: { $each: [{ id: p._id, amountMinor: p.amountMinor }], $slice: -3 } } }) } db.accounts.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }) // AP3 without an index, then with one in equality, sort, range order cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) db.payments.createIndex({ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }) cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) // leave status out: the index finds the merchant, but the sort is no longer free cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5))

try.expect:
Output trimmed to the four results that matter, and folded onto fewer lines:

{ _id: 'A-1001', customerId: 'C-77', currency: 'EUR',
  recentPayments: [ { id: 'pay-81100', amountMinor: 3817 },
                    { id: 'pay-81150', amountMinor: 725 },
                    { id: 'pay-81200', amountMinor: 7134 } ] }

{ plan: 'SORT > COLLSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 0, docsExamined: 1000 }
{ plan: 'LIMIT > FETCH > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 5, docsExamined: 5 }
{ plan: 'FETCH > SORT > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 200, docsExamined: 5 }

Five payments went in, and the list kept the last three. Read each plan from right to left. COLLSCAN is a collection scan, a read of every document. IXSCAN walks the index, FETCH loads the documents the index points at, and SORT sorts in memory. Without the index, MongoDB reads all 1,000 documents and sorts them. With it, it reads exactly 5 index entries and 5 documents. Drop status from the query, and it walks all 200 index entries for M-0042, then sorts in memory: the index is ordered by status first, so time order isn't free any more.

refs.title: MongoDB: the ESR (equality, sort, range) guideline

opening:
Picture the payments company's first week on its new store, a database spread over 40 machines. A café owner phones support: "Show me my failed payments from this morning." The support screen thinks for a while, then shows an error that says the query "might involve data filtering". Last week, on PostgreSQL, the same question came back in a few milliseconds.

It's easy to blame the new store. The SQL track taught a good habit: store each fact once, and ask any question later, because the database can always read everything if it must. On one machine, that's true. Spread over 40 machines, reading everything means asking all 40.

Why other data models exist ended on a rule: the key decides which questions are cheap. In this lesson, we'll count what three kinds of question cost, write the app's questions down before choosing a key, and design keys for them in two real stores. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café owner's question that a 40-machine store refused. Its address began with the account, and the question named a shop. The fix wasn't a faster scan. It was a second copy of the data, filed by shop, planned before the first payment arrived.

Pick an app you use, such as your bank's, and list three screens it shows you. For each one, ask what it looks things up by: you, a date, a shop? That's its access-pattern list.

Next, we'll put these keys into a real DynamoDB table, and find out how to store a payment exactly once when the card reader sends it twice.

compare.title: AP1 in PostgreSQL and in Cassandra

a.label: PostgreSQL: one table per kind of thing, join when you read
a.title: PostgreSQL: one table per kind of thing, join when you read
a.html: -- one table per kind of thing; any question can come later CREATE TABLE payment ( payment_id text PRIMARY KEY, account_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES account, merchant_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES merchant, amount_minor bigint NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX payment_acct_time ON payment (account_id, created_at DESC); SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor, m.name FROM payment p JOIN merchant m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id WHERE p.account_id = 'A-1001' ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

b.label: Cassandra: one table per query
b.title: Cassandra: one table per query
b.html: -- the query decides the table; merchant_name is copied in when the payment is written CREATE TABLE payments_by_account ( account_id text, created_at timestamp, payment_id text, merchant_name text, amount_minor bigint, PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (created_at DESC, payment_id ASC); SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, merchant_name FROM payments_by_account WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' LIMIT 20;

compare.note: Both return the same 20 payments. PostgreSQL reads them through an index and looks up the shop's name with a join when you read, so a shop that changes its name shows the new name everywhere at once. A new question tomorrow needs a new index, or none. Cassandra copies the shop's name into every payment row when it writes, so the read is one partition slice with no join. A new name then means rewriting old rows or living with the old one, and a new question means a new table.

worked.title: Design keys for the refunds part of the app

steps.say: The refunds part of the app asks three questions. Write them as data, the way the lab does. R3 serves an approvals screen that lists a shop's refunds waiting for approval, oldest first.
steps.code: val patterns = listOf( AccessPattern("R1 refunds of a payment, newest first", equals = setOf("paymentId"), orderBy = "createdAt"), AccessPattern("R2 refund by id", equals = setOf("refundId")), AccessPattern("R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first", equals = setOf("merchantId", "status"), orderBy = "createdAt"), )

steps.say: First draft: key the table by refundId, then add one index for each other question. The shop index sorts by time first, because time felt like the main thing.
steps.code: val draft = listOf( KeyIndex("table", partitionKey = listOf("refundId")), KeyIndex("byPayment", partitionKey = listOf("paymentId"), sortKey = listOf("createdAt")), KeyIndex("byMerchant", partitionKey = listOf("merchantId"), sortKey = listOf("createdAt", "status")), ) AccessPatternChecker.checkAll(patterns, draft).forEach(::println)

steps.say: R3 comes back as a scan. status = PENDING is an =, but status is the second sort attribute, after createdAt. Pending refunds are spread across the whole time range, so the store would read the shop's entire partition and filter it.
steps.code:
Verdict(pattern=R1 refunds of a payment, newest first, kind=RANGE_READ, index=byPayment)
Verdict(pattern=R2 refund by id, kind=KEY_LOOKUP, index=table)
Verdict(pattern=R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first, kind=SCAN, index=null)

steps.say: Put the = before the order: (merchantId; status, createdAt). status = PENDING now fixes the first part of the sort key, and the oldest-first order is the very next attribute. Every refund is now written three times, once per copy, and each copy answers a question on the list.
steps.code: KeyIndex("byMerchant", partitionKey = listOf("merchantId"), sortKey = listOf("status", "createdAt")) // Verdict(pattern=R3 merchant's refunds awaiting approval, oldest first, kind=RANGE_READ, index=byMerchant)

lab.title: Build an access-pattern checker, then fix the payments key design
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All nine fail for now. No Docker needed.

Write AccessPatternChecker.classify, following rules 1 to 5 in its KDoc, the comment above the function. check and checkAll are given and call it. When you're done, eight tests pass and only the design test fails.

Open PaymentsKeyDesign.kt. The table is keyed by paymentId only, so AP2 is the only pattern it answers. Add indexes until AP1 and AP3 are range reads and AP2 and AP4 are key lookups. The test also checks that every index you add answers at least one pattern.
Experiment: swap the order of the sort key in your shop index and run the tests again. Watch AP3 turn into a scan, then put it back.
hints: Rule 1 is one line: if (!pattern.equals.containsAll(index.partitionKey)) return ReadKind.SCAN.

For rule 2, count with a while loop how many sort key attributes, from the left, are in pattern.equals. Call that number fixed. Then index.sortKey.getOrNull(fixed) is the only attribute a range or an order may use.
For rule 3, build the list of usable attributes, index.partitionKey + index.sortKey.take(fixed), and check that it contains every attribute in pattern.equals.
For the design, go pattern by pattern. Whatever a pattern fixes with = goes into the partition key. For AP3, the status also goes first in the sort key, before the time.

drill.title: AP3 in CQL from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the CQL table that answers AP3 (a shop's payments with one status in a time window) with one partition per shop per day. Then write the SELECT for shop M-0042's FAILED payments on 2026-11-07 after 09:00 UTC. Check the order of your clustering columns against the answer.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE payments_by_merchant_day ( merchant_id text, day date, status text, created_at timestamp, payment_id text, account_id text, amount_minor bigint, -- (partition key), then clustering columns: equality first, then the range PRIMARY KEY ((merchant_id, day), status, created_at, payment_id) ); SELECT status, created_at, payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments_by_merchant_day WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND day = '2026-11-07' AND status = 'FAILED' AND created_at >= '2026-11-07 09:00:00+0000';

recap: In a store spread over many machines, design from the questions: list every access pattern, with how often it runs, before you choose a key.
The partition key needs = on all its parts. The sort key gives cheap slices: = on its first parts, then one range on the next, with no gaps.
Every query is a key lookup, a range read or a scan. A filter on a field outside the key still pays for everything it reads.
A pattern the key can't answer gets another copy of the data: a global secondary index in DynamoDB, another table in Cassandra, another index in MongoDB. Each copy costs a write for every new item.
In MongoDB, embed what is read together and stays small, reference what grows without end, and order compound index fields equality, sort, range.
The limit: a design answers only the questions on its list. A new question next quarter means a new copy of the data, or a scan.

explain.prompt: A teammate suggests a DynamoDB payments table keyed only by paymentId, and says: "We'll handle the other questions with filters later." Explain what happens to AP1 and AP3 at 50 million payments, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: With only paymentId in the key, the table answers one question cheaply: a payment by its id. AP1 (an account's newest payments) and AP3 (a shop's payments by status and time) don't give the partition key, so DynamoDB can't run them as a Query, its read for one partition. They become Scans with a filter, and a filter runs after the read. So each request reads all 50 million items, page by page, to return twenty. That's slow, and it uses up read capacity that the card-tap path needs. Instead, I'd write the access patterns down first and give each one a key. For AP1, a global secondary index keyed by account, with the creation time as its sort key. For AP3, one keyed by shop, with status and then time in its sort key. Each new payment then updates three copies, but every read costs what it returns.

deeper.html:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 7) splits the extra indexes of a store spread over many machines into two kinds. The split explains the designs in this lesson, and Secondary indexes across shards: local and global, in the Partitioning track, builds both.

A local index lives with each partition and indexes only that partition's data (Kleppmann calls it document-partitioned). Writes stay cheap, because a write touches one partition and its own index. But a read by the indexed field must ask every partition and merge the answers, the 40-machine question from the first section. DynamoDB's local secondary indexes are local in this sense. They share the table's partition key, so they only help queries that already know the partition. Cassandra's storage-attached indexes (SAI, new in 5.0) are local too.

A global index is split up by the indexed value itself (term-partitioned), so a read by that value goes to one place. The cost moves to writes: one payment write may have to update index partitions on other machines. DynamoDB's global secondary indexes work this way, and DynamoDB updates them a moment after the table, so a read from one can briefly miss a write the table already has. That's why they only offer reads that may be a moment behind.

Cassandra's "one table per question" is a global index you keep up by hand: you choose how each copy is split, and your code writes both. Cassandra's materialized views tried to do that for you, and they're still marked experimental, so most teams write the tables themselves.

In DynamoDB single-table design and transactions, lesson 4 of this track, one DynamoDB table holds several of these patterns at once, by giving each kind of item its own key prefix. Read DeBrie's post before then. He's in favour of it, and he lists the cases where he wouldn't use it.
